sourcingNote:
This section goes further than the other culture topics: it is also about how people in Spain live, talk and behave, not only about rules.
So it has its own rule. A statement about people either rests on a statistic or an official source, or it is marked as common practice. Under a topic you find the sources and the date they are from. Where a topic has no source list, it describes common practice: it is not a survey result, and it varies by person, age and region. We write "many" or "most", never "the Spanish are ...". Almost 49.6 million people live in Spain (INE, 1 January 2026, provisional figure), and they are all different: young and old, from Galicia to Andalusia, from big cities and from villages, born in Spain or abroad.
Where something is debated, both sides are shown. Rules and figures change; if in doubt, the linked official source is right.

topics.title: Saying hello: dos besos, handshake, ¡Buenas!
topics.intro: In Spain, people often greet each other with words first, and friends often give dos besos (two kisses on the cheeks). At work, a handshake is normal when you meet someone for the first time. Many people also say hello to neighbours in the lift and to staff when they enter a shop.
topics.question: ¿Cómo saludas en tu país? (How do you greet people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age, the region and the place.

Dos besos: one light kiss on each cheek, often without a real kiss, just cheek to cheek. It is common between two women and between a woman and a man who know each other, and between friends and family.
At work, people shake hands at a first meeting and say “Mucho gusto” or “Encantado/a”. With colleagues you see every day, “Hola” or “Buenos días” is enough.
“¡Buenas!” is a short, friendly greeting for any time of day. People use it when they enter a bar or a shop, and in the lift.
When you leave a shop or a bar, many people say “Hasta luego” or “Adiós”, even to people they will not see again.
topics.context: If you are not sure, wait for the other person. If they lean in for dos besos, do the same. If they put out a hand, shake it. Nobody will mind a small mistake.
phrases: Hola, mucho gusto. (Hello, nice to meet you.)
¡Buenas! (Hello! Said when you come in.)
¿Qué tal? (How are you?)
Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? (Fine, thanks. And you?)
Buenos días a todos. (Good morning, everybody.)
Hasta luego. (See you later.)

quiz.prompt: You meet your new boss for the first time. What do most people do?
quiz.answer: Shake hands
quiz.explain: A handshake is normal at a first meeting at work.

quiz.prompt: You enter a small shop. Which short greeting fits?
quiz.answer: ¡Buenas!
quiz.explain: “¡Buenas!” is a friendly greeting when you come in. “Hasta luego” is for leaving.

quiz.prompt: What are dos besos?
options: One light kiss on each cheek
quiz.answer: One light kiss on each cheek
quiz.explain: Dos besos is a common greeting between friends and family, and between many people who know each other.

topics.title: Queues and personal space
topics.intro: In Spain, people usually wait in order in shops, at the market and at the doctor, but the line is often not a straight line. You ask who is last and then you know your turn. Many people also stand closer and touch an arm when they talk, and a bar can be very loud.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se espera en tu país? (How do people wait in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the place and the situation.
In a shop with no clear line, you ask “¿Quién es el último?” (Who is last?). Someone says “Yo”. After that you know who is before you.
Many people stand closer to each other than in some other countries, and they may touch your arm or shoulder when they talk. It is usually friendly.
A bar at lunchtime can be very loud. People talk loudly across the room, and this is normal. It is not an argument.
If you touch someone by accident, say “Perdón”. You can also say it when you want to pass: “Perdona, ¿puedo pasar?”
topics.context: At the doctor’s or the town hall, there is sometimes a ticket machine with numbers. If not, ask “¿Quién es el último?” when you arrive, and say “Yo soy el último” to the next person.
phrases: ¿Quién es el último? (Who is last?)
Yo. (I am. Said by the last person.)
Perdona, ¿puedo pasar? (Excuse me, can I get past?)
Perdón. (Sorry.)
Yo estaba antes. (I was here before.)

quiz.prompt: You enter a shop with no clear line. What do you ask?
quiz.answer: ¿Quién es el último?
quiz.explain: You ask who is last, then you know when it is your turn.

quiz.prompt: A person touches your arm while talking. What is it often?
quiz.answer: A friendly gesture
quiz.explain: Many people touch an arm when they talk. It is usually friendly.

quiz.prompt: You push past someone by accident. What do you say?
quiz.answer: Perdón.
quiz.explain: “Perdón” or “Perdona” is the normal word for a small mistake.

topics.title: Please and thank you
topics.intro: In Spain, politeness is often in the tone, the greeting and the thanks, not in many “por favor”. A short order like “Ponme una caña” is normal in a bar and is not rude. Learn a few small words, such as vale and perdona, and you will sound natural.
topics.question: ¿Cómo pides las cosas en tu país? (How do you ask for things in your country?)

table.label: What you say, and what it does
rows: Ponme una caña.
A normal, friendly order in a bar. You can add “por favor” if you want.
Perdona. / Perdone.
Gets someone’s attention, or says sorry for a small thing. Perdone is more formal.
Vale.
OK, agreed, understood. Very common and polite.
Gracias.
Thank you. People say it often when they pay, leave and get something.
¿Me pones…? / ¿Me das…?
Asking for something in a shop, soft and normal.
Con permiso.
Excuse me, I am passing. Said in a lift or a crowded place.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the age and the situation.
In a bar or a shop, a short order such as “Ponme un café” is normal, friendly and not rude. Many people also say “por favor” and “gracias”, but not in every sentence.
People often use the present tense or a question for requests: “¿Me pones un café?”, and not a long polite phrase.
A friendly tone, a greeting and “gracias” at the end matter more than the number of “por favor”.
With older people or in formal situations, use usted and add “por favor”.
topics.context: If a native speaker sounds short, it is usually not anger. Listen to the tone, the face and the greeting. A smile and “gracias” make a short sentence warm.
phrases: Ponme una caña, por favor. (A small beer, please.)
¿Me pones un café con leche? (Could I have a coffee with milk?)
Perdona, ¿tienes hora? (Excuse me, do you have the time?)
Vale, perfecto. (OK, great.)
Muchas gracias, que tengas un buen día. (Thank you, have a good day.)
Perdone, ¿me puede ayudar? (Excuse me, can you help me?)

quiz.prompt: In a bar, you say “Ponme un café.” How is it often seen?
quiz.answer: Normal and friendly
quiz.explain: A short order is normal in a bar. A greeting and “gracias” make it warm.

quiz.prompt: What does “Vale” mean?
quiz.answer: OK, agreed
quiz.explain: “Vale” is a very common word for OK and agreed.

quiz.prompt: You want to get past a person in a crowded place. Which phrase fits?
quiz.answer: Con permiso.
quiz.explain: “Con permiso” means excuse me, I am passing. “Que aproveche” is for someone who eats.

topics.title: Time and timing
topics.intro: In Spain, meals are often later than in many other countries, and a little lateness among friends is common. At work and at the doctor, people usually expect you on time. Some small words, such as “ahora voy” and “mañana”, are less exact than they sound.
topics.question: ¿Qué pasa si llegas tarde en tu país? (What happens if you are late in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the region, the age and the situation.
Many people have lunch (la comida) around 14:00 or 15:00 and dinner (la cena) around 21:00 or 22:00. A dinner invitation at 21:30 is not unusual.
Among friends, 10 or 15 minutes late is often normal. If you are later, send a message: “Llego en diez minutos”.
At work, in a job interview and at the doctor or the town hall, be on time. Cita previa (a booked appointment) means a fixed time.
“Ahora voy” can mean “I am coming soon”, but not always “right now”. “Mañana” can mean tomorrow, or just “not today”. If it is important, ask for a day or an hour.
topics.context: If you are late, say so early and say why in a short sentence. A short message is better than silence.
phrases: ¿A qué hora quedamos? (What time shall we meet?)
Llego en diez minutos. (I will be there in ten minutes.)
Perdona el retraso. (Sorry for being late.)
Ahora voy. (I am coming soon.)
¿Mañana a qué hora, exactamente? (Tomorrow at what time, exactly?)
Tengo cita a las diez. (I have an appointment at ten.)

quiz.prompt: You have a doctor’s appointment at ten. When do you arrive?
options: At ten, or a bit before
quiz.answer: At ten, or a bit before
quiz.explain: At the doctor and at work, people usually expect you on time.

quiz.prompt: A friend says “Ahora voy.” What can it mean?
options: I am coming soon, not always right now
quiz.answer: I am coming soon, not always right now
quiz.explain: “Ahora voy” is not always exact. Ask for a time if it is important.

quiz.prompt: What is a normal time for dinner (la cena) for many people?
quiz.answer: 21:00 or later
quiz.explain: Many people eat dinner around 21:00 or 22:00.

topics.title: Paying the bill
topics.intro: In Spain, friends often take turns to pay, and one person may say “Hoy invito yo” (I pay today). Splitting the bill equally, called a escote, is also common. It is normal to argue in a friendly way about who pays.
topics.question: ¿Quién paga en tu país cuando se sale en grupo? (Who pays in your country when people go out together?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.
“Invitar” means to pay for the others. “Hoy invito yo” means I pay today. Next time, someone else pays: “Ahora me toca a mí”.
“A escote” means everybody pays the same share. In a bar with friends, one person often pays a round (una ronda) and then another person.
Offering to pay once or twice is normal. People say “No, no, invito yo” and the other person says “Venga, pago yo”. After that, you can accept and say thanks.
In a restaurant, you ask for the bill with “La cuenta, por favor”. Many people use Bizum, a mobile payment between bank accounts, to send their share by phone.
topics.context: If you do not want to pay for others, say it early and clearly: “Yo pago lo mío”. Most people understand this.
phrases: La cuenta, por favor. (The bill, please.)
Hoy invito yo. (I pay today.)
Vamos a escote. (Let’s split it equally.)
Te hago un Bizum. (I will send you the money by Bizum.)
Ahora me toca a mí. (Now it is my turn.)
Yo pago lo mío. (I pay my own part.)

quiz.prompt: A friend says “Hoy invito yo.” What does that mean?
quiz.answer: I pay today
quiz.explain: “Invitar” in this situation means to pay for the others.

quiz.prompt: What does “a escote” mean?
quiz.answer: Everybody pays the same share
quiz.explain: A escote is an equal split of the bill.

quiz.prompt: What is Bizum?
options: A payment from phone to phone
quiz.answer: A payment from phone to phone
quiz.explain: Bizum sends money between bank accounts by mobile phone, for example your share of a bill.

topics.title: Small talk and sobremesa
topics.intro: In Spain, many people meet and talk in a bar, at an aperitivo before lunch, or at the table after a meal. This talk after eating is called the sobremesa, and it can last a long time. Small talk is easy with food, family, travel and football.
topics.question: ¿De qué se habla con gente nueva en tu país? (What do people talk about with new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the place.
El aperitivo is a drink and a small snack before lunch, often at the weekend. It is a normal way to meet friends or colleagues.
La sobremesa is the time at the table after the meal. People stay, talk and have coffee. Leaving right after the last bite can look hasty.
Safe topics for a first talk: food, where you are from, travel, work, family, football, the weather, and the place you live.
Many people avoid strong opinions about politics, religion or money with people they do not know well. Questions about salary are usually too personal at first.
topics.context: People may ask questions that feel personal, for example if you have children. Usually it is interest, not a test. You can answer short or say “Prefiero no hablar de eso”.
phrases: ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
¿Y tú, a qué te dedicas? (And you, what do you do?)
¿Te apetece tomar algo? (Do you fancy a drink?)
Qué rico está esto. (This is really tasty.)
Llevo un año en España. (I have been in Spain for a year.)
¿Vemos el partido en el bar? (Shall we watch the match in the bar?)

quiz.prompt: What is la sobremesa?
options: Time at the table after the meal
quiz.answer: Time at the table after the meal
quiz.explain: People stay, talk and have coffee after the meal.

quiz.prompt: Which topic is usually safe for a first talk?
quiz.answer: Food and travel
quiz.explain: Food, travel and football are easy topics. Salary and politics are more personal.

quiz.prompt: When is the aperitivo?
quiz.answer: Before lunch
quiz.explain: El aperitivo is a drink and a snack before the meal, often at the weekend.

topics.title: Making friends
topics.intro: In Spain, friendships often start in small groups: the building, the neighbourhood, a club, a language exchange or the school gate. You often meet people in a WhatsApp group first, and then in a bar. It takes time, but small steps help.
topics.question: ¿Dónde conoces gente nueva en tu país? (Where do you meet new people in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the city, the age and the person.
Many buildings have a WhatsApp group for neighbours. It is useful for news, noise and small problems. Say hello in it and keep your messages short.
The comunidad de vecinos is the group of owners in a building. They hold meetings (juntas) about costs and repairs. Tenants are often not at the meeting, but the landlord is.
A peña is a club of friends around a football team, a festival, a hobby or a town party. Many towns have several.
Language exchanges (intercambios) are a common way to meet people. At the school gate, parents often have a WhatsApp group for their class.
topics.context: Plans in Spain often start with “A ver si quedamos”. Say a day: “¿Qué tal el sábado?” A concrete offer makes a friendship start.
phrases: ¿Os apetece tomar algo? (Do you fancy a drink, you all?)
Soy tu vecino del tercero. (I am your neighbour from the third floor.)
¿Hay algún grupo de WhatsApp del edificio? (Is there a WhatsApp group for the building?)
¿Quedamos el sábado? (Shall we meet on Saturday?)
Busco un intercambio de idiomas. (I am looking for a language exchange.)
¿Puedo apuntarme a la peña? (Can I join the club?)

quiz.prompt: What is a peña?
options: A club of friends around a shared interest
quiz.answer: A club of friends around a shared interest
quiz.explain: A peña can be about a football team, a festival or a hobby.

quiz.prompt: What is the comunidad de vecinos?
options: The group of owners in a building
quiz.answer: The group of owners in a building
quiz.explain: It decides about costs and repairs in the building.

quiz.prompt: You want to turn “A ver si quedamos” into a plan. What helps?
quiz.answer: Say a day
quiz.explain: A concrete offer, for example “¿Qué tal el sábado?”, makes the plan real.

topics.title: How hiring works
topics.intro: In Spain, many employers look at your currículum, and they often also use their own contacts. A photo on the CV is still common, although it is not required. Job portals, personal networks and the public employment service all play a part.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se busca trabajo en tu país? (How do people look for work in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the sector, the company, the region and the age of the applicant.
Many CVs still have a photo, although it is not required and some employers prefer none. You can ask a person in your field what is usual.
Job portals such as InfoJobs and LinkedIn are widely used, and the public employment service (SEPE and the regional services) also offers vacancies.
Personal contacts count. Getting a job through a contact is sometimes called “enchufe”, a word that is often used critically, but asking people you know for tips is normal.
Many contracts have a period of probation (período de prueba). Its length depends on the law and on the convenio colectivo (the sector agreement). Read your contract and ask.

pros: A personal contact can open a door, and a tip from a friend is quick.
A short CV is easy to read and compare.
Many employers call you early on, so things can move fast.
cons: People without a network in Spain can feel left out.
A photo, age or name can influence some employers, although discrimination is not allowed by law.
The probation period can be unclear if you do not read the contract.

topics.context: Tell people you know that you are looking for work. Many vacancies are found by word of mouth, and you can still apply on the portals in parallel.
phrases: Estoy buscando trabajo en el sector de la hostelería. (I am looking for work in hospitality.)
Le envío mi currículum. (I am sending you my CV.)
¿Cuánto dura el período de prueba? (How long is the probation period?)
¿Qué convenio colectivo se aplica? (Which collective agreement applies?)
Trabajé tres años en una tienda. (I worked for three years in a shop.)
Si quiere, puedo empezar el lunes. (If you like, I can start on Monday.)

quiz.prompt: What is an “enchufe” in the context of hiring?
options: A job through a personal contact
quiz.answer: A job through a personal contact
quiz.explain: The word is often used critically, but asking people you know for tips is normal.

quiz.prompt: Where can you find the length of a probation period?
options: In the law, the convenio and your contract
quiz.answer: In the law, the convenio and your contract
quiz.explain: The length depends on the law and on the sector agreement. Read your contract and ask.

quiz.prompt: Is a photo on the CV required in Spain?
options: No, but it is still common
No, and it is never used
quiz.answer: No, but it is still common
quiz.explain: Many CVs have a photo, but it is not required.

topics.title: Cars, trains and getting around
topics.intro: In Spain, how you travel depends on where you live: in big cities many people use metro, bus and Cercanías trains, and between cities the AVE high-speed train is popular. In smaller places, a car is often needed. Speed limits, alcohol limits and low-emission zones are part of daily life for drivers.
topics.question: ¿Cómo te mueves en tu ciudad? (How do you get around in your city?)
facts: Cercanías are the commuter trains around large cities. The AVE is the high-speed train between big cities. Both are run by Renfe, and other operators also run high-speed lines.
On motorways (autopistas and autovías) the general speed limit for cars is 120 km/h. Signs can show a lower limit.

In towns, the general limit is 30 km/h on streets with one lane in each direction, 20 km/h on streets where road and pavement are on one level, and 50 km/h on streets with two or more lanes per direction. Town halls can set other limits with signs (DGT, since 11 May 2021).

The general blood alcohol limit for drivers is 0.5 g/l (0.25 mg/l in exhaled air). Novice and professional drivers have a lower limit (0.3 g/l as of 2026). A lower limit for everyone has been under discussion, so check dgt.es.
The ITV (inspección técnica de vehículos) is the regular technical check for a car. Many cities also have zonas de bajas emisiones (low-emission zones) with rules for older cars.
A driving licence from another country: whether you can use it or must exchange it depends on the country. Check the DGT page for your licence.

prosCons.prosLabel: Why many people like the car
pros: It is flexible for villages, shift work and trips with children.
In many regions, public transport is rare outside the big towns.
It saves time on routes without a direct train.
prosCons.consLabel: Why many people prefer public transport
cons: Parking, fuel and low-emission zones cost time and money.
In cities, metro, bus and Cercanías are often faster at rush hour.
A train lets you read or work on the way.

topics.context: If you plan to drive, check three things early: your licence, the insurance and the environmental label of the car if you enter a big city. Ask at the DGT or on dgt.es.
phrases: ¿Cómo llego a la estación de Cercanías? (How do I get to the Cercanías station?)
Un billete de ida y vuelta a Sevilla, por favor. (A return ticket to Seville, please.)
¿Dónde puedo aparcar por aquí? (Where can I park around here?)
Mi coche ha pasado la ITV. (My car has passed the ITV.)
¿Puedo cambiar mi carné de conducir? (Can I exchange my driving licence?)
No he bebido nada, voy a conducir. (I have not drunk anything, I am driving.)

sources.label: DGT Revista: Cómo se aplica el 30 km/h en las ciudades

quiz.prompt: What is the general limit on a city street with one lane in each direction?
quiz.answer: 30 km/h
quiz.explain: Since May 2021 the general limit is 30 km/h on such streets, unless signs say otherwise.

quiz.prompt: What is the ITV?
options: The regular technical check for a car
quiz.answer: The regular technical check for a car
quiz.explain: ITV is inspección técnica de vehículos.

quiz.prompt: Can you always use a foreign licence in Spain?
options: It depends on the country of the licence
quiz.answer: It depends on the country of the licence
quiz.explain: Whether you can use it or must exchange it depends on the country. Check dgt.es.

topics.title: Women and men at work
topics.intro: In Spain, the law gives both parents the same paid leave for a birth, and most people keep two surnames for life. A pay gap between women and men remains in the statistics. Many people debate how to close it and how much comes from part-time work and care duties.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se reparten el trabajo y los cuidados en tu país? (How are work and care shared in your country?)
facts: Both parents have the same paid leave for the birth or adoption of a child. The leave is individual and cannot be passed to the other parent. It was extended to 19 weeks per parent for births from mid-2025 (as of 2026); check the details on seg-social.es.
People in Spain have two surnames, one from each parent. Parents can agree on the order. A woman keeps her own surnames after marriage.
According to the INE, women’s average annual earnings in 2024 were 26,904.90 euros and men’s were 32,057.55 euros. Women’s pay was 83.9 % of men’s.
This is the unadjusted gap. The INE says the difference should be read together with other variables such as type of contract, working hours, occupation and years in the company.
Part-time work is more common among women, according to labour statistics, and this is one reason which is often given for the gap. Experts discuss how large the other parts of the gap are.

prosCons.prosLabel: What many people point to as progress
pros: Equal, individual leave for both parents supports shared care.
Public data on pay makes the debate more factual.
Two surnames and the surname rule treat mothers and fathers alike on paper.
prosCons.consLabel: What many people say is still open
cons: The gap in average earnings remains.
Care work still falls more often on women.
People disagree about the reasons and about the best measures.

topics.context: If you are an employee and have a question about leave or pay, ask the human resources department (recursos humanos), your union, or the Seguridad Social. Do not rely on the opinion of a colleague alone.
phrases: Quiero pedir el permiso por nacimiento. (I want to ask for the birth leave.)
Mi mujer y yo nos hemos repartido los cuidados. (My wife and I have shared the care.)
Mis apellidos son García y López. (My surnames are García and López.)
¿Cuántas horas tiene la jornada parcial? (How many hours is the part-time day?)
Cobramos lo mismo por el mismo trabajo. (We are paid the same for the same work.)

sources.label: INE: Encuesta Anual de Estructura Salarial 2024

quiz.prompt: What is true of the paid leave for a birth?
options: Both parents have an individual right
quiz.answer: Both parents have an individual right
quiz.explain: The leave is the same for both parents and cannot be passed on.

quiz.prompt: How many surnames do people usually have?
quiz.answer: Two
quiz.explain: Most people have one surname from each parent.

quiz.prompt: In 2024, women’s average annual pay was what share of men’s (INE)?
quiz.explain: 26,904.90 euros compared with 32,057.55 euros. This is the unadjusted figure.

topics.title: Dating basics
topics.intro: In Spain, people often start with quedar, which means to arrange to meet, and then tomar algo, which means to have a drink or a bite. Many adults meet through friends, work, hobbies or dating apps. Be clear, be respectful, and listen to the other person’s answer.
topics.question: ¿Cómo se queda para una primera cita en tu país? (How do people arrange a first date in your country?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It varies by person, age, region and city.
“Quedar” means to arrange to meet. “¿Quedamos para tomar algo?” is a relaxed invitation to a drink or a coffee, and it is an easy first plan.
Many adults use dating apps such as Tinder or Bumble, but also meet through friends, at work or in clubs.
Who pays varies. Some people split, some take turns, and sometimes one person invites the first time. Say what you prefer in a friendly way: “¿Pagamos a medias?”.
Meeting friends or family usually comes later, when the relationship is clearer. “No” or “No me apetece” is a full answer, and it should be respected.
topics.context: Be honest and clear about what you want. If you do not want a second date, you can say it kindly: “Me lo he pasado muy bien, pero no creo que sea lo que busco”.
phrases: ¿Quedamos mañana para tomar algo? (Shall we meet tomorrow for a drink?)
Me lo he pasado muy bien. (I had a really good time.)
¿Pagamos a medias? (Shall we split it?)
Prefiero que vayamos poco a poco. (I prefer to go slowly.)
Me gustaría presentarte a mis amigos. (I would like to introduce you to my friends.)
Gracias por la cita, pero no busco nada serio. (Thanks for the date, but I am not looking for anything serious.)

quiz.prompt: What does “¿Quedamos para tomar algo?” mean?
options: Shall we meet for a drink?
quiz.answer: Shall we meet for a drink?
quiz.explain: Quedar means to arrange to meet. Tomar algo means to have a drink or a bite.

quiz.prompt: Who pays on a first date?
options: It varies, so you can say what you prefer
quiz.answer: It varies, so you can say what you prefer
quiz.explain: People split, take turns or invite. Say it kindly.

quiz.prompt: The other person says “No me apetece.” What should you do?
quiz.answer: Respect it
quiz.explain: A “no” is a full answer.

topics.title: Direct and indirect
topics.intro: In Spain, some everyday phrases are softer than they sound. A “ya te diré” is often a gentle no or “not yet”, and a plan that starts with “a ver si quedamos” may stay open. At the same time, a plain “no” in a bar is normal and not rude.
topics.question: ¿Cómo dices que no sin ofender? (How do you say no without offending?)

table.label: What is said, and what it can mean
rows: Ya te diré.
Often “I will decide later”, and sometimes a soft no. Ask for a day.
A ver si quedamos.
A friendly wish to meet, without a fixed plan. Suggest a day if you want to meet.
Hombre…
A soft start to disagree or to correct, as in “Hombre, no sé…”.
No te preocupes.
It is fine, I will manage, or please do not worry. The tone shows which one.
Lo vamos viendo.
No decision yet. It may need a follow-up from you.
No, gracias.
A clear and polite no, for example when the waiter offers dessert. It is not rude.

facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the person, the region, the age and the relationship.
In a bar or a shop, a plain “no” or “no, gracias” is normal and not rude. You do not need a long excuse.
Between friends and colleagues, strong opinions and interruptions are often a sign of interest in the topic, not of anger.
In invitations, “a ver si quedamos” is often a polite wish. A day or an hour in the next sentence turns it into a real plan.
If you are not sure what a phrase means, ask in a friendly way: “¿Entonces, quedamos el jueves?”
topics.context: Style varies a lot by region and person. If a phrase is unclear, repeat it in your own words, or suggest a concrete day. This is clearer for both sides and is not rude.
phrases: Ya te diré algo mañana. (I will tell you something tomorrow.)
A ver si quedamos un día de estos. (Let’s meet one of these days.)
Hombre, no sé si es buena idea. (Well, I am not sure it is a good idea.)
No te preocupes, ya lo hago yo. (Don’t worry, I will do it.)
¿Entonces, quedamos el jueves o no? (So, are we meeting on Thursday or not?)
No, gracias, ya estoy servido. (No, thanks, I have had enough.)

quiz.prompt: A colleague says “A ver si quedamos.” What is it most often?
options: A friendly wish without a date
quiz.answer: A friendly wish without a date
quiz.explain: Suggest a day if you want to turn it into a plan.

quiz.prompt: At a bar the waiter offers dessert. You say “No, gracias.” How is this seen?
quiz.answer: Polite and clear
quiz.explain: A plain no is normal. You do not need an excuse.

quiz.prompt: Someone says “Ya te diré.” What can it mean?
options: I will decide later, or a soft no
quiz.answer: I will decide later, or a soft no
quiz.explain: If it matters, ask for a day to hear the answer.

topics.title: Humour and banter
topics.intro: In Spain, many people use humour to build closeness: vacilar (to tease in fun), estar de coña (to be joking) and irony are common among friends and colleagues. Jokes about regions are also common, so listen first and join in only when you know the people. In Cádiz, the carnival groups called chirigotas turn current topics into songs.
topics.question: ¿Con quién bromeas y con quién no? (Who do you joke with and who not?)
facts: This is common practice, not a survey result. It changes with the group, the age and the situation.
“Vacilar” (a bit informal) means to tease someone in fun. “Estar de coña” or “de broma” means to be joking. “Es coña” tells people it was not serious.
Irony is common: someone may say “Qué bien” when something is bad. Tone and face show it.
Jokes about regions, for example about accents or food, are often heard. They are not welcome in every case. If you are new, do not start them. Wait until you know the people.
Chirigotas are carnival groups from Cádiz. They write songs with humour about current events, and they perform at the carnival, in February or early March.

pros: Teasing between friends is a sign of trust.
Irony makes difficult things easier to say.
Satire in carnival songs is a long local tradition.
cons: A joke that works in one group may hurt in another.
As a newcomer, you may not know the limits yet.
Jokes about origin, religion or looks can hurt, even if the speaker means well.

topics.context: Join the banter with a small, kind joke about yourself first, such as your Spanish mistakes. If someone looks upset, say “Era broma, perdona”.
phrases: Estás de coña, ¿no? (You are joking, aren’t you?)
No me vaciles. (Don’t tease me.)
Era broma, perdona. (It was a joke, sorry.)
Qué bueno, me he reído un montón. (That was good, I laughed a lot.)
A mí esa broma no me hace gracia. (That joke is not funny to me.)
Mi español es un desastre, pero lo intento. (My Spanish is a disaster, but I am trying.)

quiz.prompt: What does “estar de coña” mean?
quiz.answer: To be joking
quiz.explain: “Es coña” tells people that it was not serious.

quiz.prompt: You are new in a group. A joke about a region comes up. What is sensible?

Listen first and join only when you know the people
quiz.answer: Listen first and join only when you know the people
quiz.explain: Regional jokes are common, but they depend on the group.

quiz.prompt: What are chirigotas?

quiz.answer: Carnival groups from Cádiz with humorous songs
quiz.explain: They sing about current events at the carnival, in February or early March.
